groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: What does Brewster want to improve?

evidence.summary: Brewster aims to make the cars more visible because unnoticed danger can cause accidents.

distractors.B: The project concerns noticing danger, not encouraging taxi travel.
distractors.C: Passenger capacity is not the problem identified.

options.label: A
options.text: How visible driverless cars are to road users.

options.label: B
options.text: How often pedestrians travel by taxi.

options.label: C
options.text: How many people can sit in the car.

questions.prompt: Which two approaches did the team test?

evidence.summary: The research compared moving displays with fixed coloured rings.

distractors.A: Eye contact and gestures describe existing human communication, not the two tested devices.
distractors.B: The two methods named are visual animations and light rings.

options.label: A
options.text: Eye contact and human hand signals.

options.label: B
options.text: Sound recordings and road signs.

options.label: C
options.text: Animations and fixed coloured light rings.

questions.prompt: Why are animations less useful for runners and cyclists?

evidence.summary: Faster-moving users have only a brief look and may miss the animation.

distractors.A: No general ban on crossing is stated for these users.
distractors.C: The account identifies limited viewing time, not an inability to distinguish colours.

options.label: A
options.text: They are not allowed to cross roads.

options.label: B
options.text: They have less time to look and make a decision.

options.label: C
options.text: They are unable to see any colours.

evidence.summary: Pippa suggests familiarity may help people learn how and when to cross.

distractors.C: Her suggestion concerns experience with the technology, not hiding it.

options.label: A

options.label: B

tests.title: Communicating intent: interpreting the limits of a signal

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: Which direct visual interaction is lost when a human driver is absent? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: Eye contact with a driver is one means of negotiating passage unavailable in an empty driving seat.

evidence.summary: His proposed response is to go behind the vehicle after it has passed.

questions.prompt: What type of fixed signal was tested alongside animations? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The team tested fixed coloured light rings as an alternative to animations.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: Group for which the animation result was positive: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The reported success for animations is specifically attributed to pedestrians.

questions.prompt: Brief viewing opportunity that may miss the moving message: a {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The researcher uses a glance to explain why a moving message may not be registered.

questions.prompt: Hazard the warning is intended to draw attention to: a {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Alerting road users is explained as warning them about a potential danger.

groups.heading: Questions 7–8
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: Which design conclusion follows from the account without overgeneralising?

evidence.summary: The contrast shows that signal design needs to account for the observer's available viewing time.

distractors.A: The account says animations work well for pedestrians.
distractors.C: The researcher explicitly distinguishes faster users from pedestrians.

options.label: A
options.text: The need for rings establishes that pedestrians cannot interpret moving images.

options.label: B
options.text: A signal useful for pedestrians may be poorly suited to someone who can look only briefly.

options.label: C
options.text: The success with pedestrians establishes that animations suit every road user.

questions.prompt: Which interpretation captures the cultural problem rather than the earlier speed problem?

evidence.summary: The cultural example concerns meaning changing even when the physical gesture is the same.

distractors.B: That is the earlier temporal problem, not the difference in cultural meaning asked about.
distractors.C: That concerns the design response to limited time rather than cultural interpretation.

options.label: A
options.text: Identical hand movements can convey different intentions to different observers.

options.label: B
options.text: A moving image may not be fully seen during a short glance.

options.label: C
options.text: A coloured ring can be noticed more quickly than a full animation.

tests.title: Different users, different signals: close listening

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: Negotiation with a conventional driver can begin with {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The opening explanation identifies eye contact as part of negotiating movement with a driver.

questions.prompt: In an autonomous vehicle there is nobody in the {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The missing person in the driving seat removes the familiar human communication partner.

questions.prompt: Rather than assuming it will yield, Phil suggests waiting and going {{blank}} the robotaxi.

evidence.summary: Phil's tentative strategy is to wait for the vehicle and cross behind it.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: How certain is Pippa about people adapting to the technology?

evidence.summary: Pippa uses tentative language to suggest a role for growing familiarity rather than guaranteeing it.

distractors.B: Her language concerns a possible future change, not universal present understanding.
distractors.C: She explicitly suggests familiarity may improve how people deal with it.

options.label: A
options.text: She tentatively suggests that greater familiarity may help.

options.label: B
options.text: She states that every road user already understands it.

options.label: C
options.text: She rejects experience as a possible influence on confidence.

questions.prompt: Why is making the vehicle noticeable part of Brewster's approach?

evidence.summary: The project links the visibility intervention to the risk of unnoticed approaching danger.

distractors.A: The cause given is not seeing oncoming danger, not destination uncertainty.
distractors.B: The goal of visibility is not a guarantee about yielding behaviour.

options.label: A
options.text: All accidents are attributed to uncertainty about the destination.

options.label: B
options.text: Being visible is said to guarantee that a vehicle will always yield.

options.label: C
options.text: Failure to notice approaching danger is identified as a cause of accidents.

questions.prompt: Which interpretation preserves the distinction in the experiment's results?

evidence.summary: The result is user-dependent because the time available to take in the display differs.

distractors.A: The result differs for runners and cyclists, motivating an alternative.
distractors.C: The result for pedestrians is explicitly positive.

options.label: A
options.text: Animations succeeded equally for every group, making the rings redundant.

options.label: B
options.text: Animations can work for walkers while conveying too little during a cyclist's brief look.

options.label: C
options.text: Animations failed for pedestrians, so fixed rings were designed only for them.
